A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, optimization framework, neural datasets, and core analyses. The complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original RNN comparisons, decoding experiments, optimization dynamics, and principal-component perturbation simulations in Figures 2–6.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and reports additional decoding, regularization-sensitivity, and neural-data perturbation results in Figures 3, 6, and S2.

M1.justification: The method still optimizes Gaussian-initialized synthetic data through differentiable similarity scores using Adam, including joint optimization of score pairs. The RNN architectures are unchanged. Expanded metric descriptions and disclosure of differentiation through PyTorch's lstsq do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: The five source datasets are retained, but functional decoding coverage expands substantially. Beyond v1's Mante/Siegel decision variables, v2 Figure 3 evaluates eight reaching directions, eight object categories, and texture-versus-noise classification using Hatsopoulos, MajajHong, and FreemanZiemba recordings.

E2.justification: v2 extends the Mante/Siegel decoding comparisons to angular CKA, NBS, and unregularized linear regression alongside the original three measures. These methods already appeared in other v1 analyses. The condition-average reference disappears from the corresponding decoding plots, although it remains in Figure 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a decoding-summary threshold at 90% of the improvement from chance to neural-data accuracy. Its new ridge experiment evaluates lambda values 1, 10, 100, 1000, and 10000 rather than only the previously reported default of 100. Existing five-fold decoding and regression protocols remain documented.

E4.justification: Figure S2 adds a substantive regularization-sensitivity analysis. Figure 6 replaces the single synthetic PC-perturbation example with validation on five neural datasets. Section 4.1 also briefly reports removing low-variance PCs to investigate above-reference decoding accuracy; this control did not resolve the observation.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces explicit repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing error bars and shaded bands remain without a newly documented uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds decoding curves and threshold results across more tasks and measures, regularization-dependent decoding outcomes in Figure S2, and five neural-data perturbation results replacing v1's synthetic example. Figures 2, 4, and 5 largely retain their results, and v1 Figure 3's decoding curves reappear in Figure S1.

T1.justification: The perturbation assumptions and CKA/NBS derivation in v1 Appendix B.3 are retained in v2 Appendix C.2. The angular Procrustes rescaling already appeared in v1. v2 reorganizes and expands explanations of these relationships without adding a substantive theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims about misleadingly high similarity, variance sensitivity, and dependencies between measures remain. v2 explicitly adds dataset dependence to its claim about good-score thresholds and qualifies the introduction's angular-Procrustes/CKA implication to the illustrated dataset, refining the scope of the conclusions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly rejects universal metric superiority and acknowledges that optimization dynamics combine optimizer behavior with similarity-measure behavior, materially qualifying the interpretation. It also introduces a tentative denoising explanation for above-reference decoding and reports that simply removing low-variance PCs does not explain it.

D1.justification: v2 adds the PyTorch lstsq implementation detail, explicit binarization information, and further explanation of joint-score optimization. Project, code, and package access addresses change. Conversely, v1's NVIDIA GeForce GTX TITAN X and less-than-one-day compute disclosure is removed. Much other apparent documentation growth is relocated material.

R1.justification: The reference to Cloos et al. 2022 on RNN evaluation is removed, while Cloos et al. 2024 on standardizing similarity measures is added. Related work additionally emphasizes joint-score optimization, but the principal comparisons with earlier similarity-measure research remain.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introductory framing, adds an explicit contribution list, restructures the methods, and rewrites Sections 4.1 and 4.3. Optimization details move from the appendix into Section 3.2, while lengthy Figure 2 explanations move into the appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds a five-panel decoding Figure 3 and Figure S2, relocates the earlier Figure 3 to S1, expands the perturbation display, and separates joint-score diagrams into Figure 7. The latter removes displayed optimization trajectories. Captions, diagram arrangement, and the document's title and heading layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the practical conclusions: functional decoding extends beyond two contextual-decision examples, the ridge sweep tests dependence on regularization, and neural-data perturbations support theory previously illustrated synthetically. Explicit dataset-dependent thresholds and the optimizer-confounding limitation make the conclusions better supported and more carefully bounded. These gains outweigh the limited reproducibility loss from removing hardware and compute-time information; uncertainty reporting remains a weakness.
